extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of mathematical logic (advanced undergraduate / beginning graduate level)
extracted.subtask_description: Formal development and proof of the completeness theorem for first-order logic (Henkin expansion, term model, factoring for identity), together with compactness and Löwenheim–Skolem results; includes definitions and constructions used in those proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 112B — membership and implication in complete consistent sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose Γ is complete and consistent. Then: (1) If Γ ⊢ α, then α ∈ Γ. (2) α → β ∈ Γ iff either α ∉ Γ or β ∈ Γ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to move between provability and membership for complete consistent sets. The proof uses completeness of Γ to deduce negations and standard properties of ⊢ (reflexivity, monotonicity, transitivity); item (1) is used repeatedly in later truth-lemma arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Henkin expansion (witnessing trick)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expand the language by adding infinitely many new constant symbols and for each wff α(x) with one free variable adjoin a sentence of the form ¬∀x α(x) → ¬α(c) where c is a new constant symbol. This guarantees that any false universal sentence has a counterexample among the new constants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This construction ensures the existence of 'witness' constants and is the central device for building saturated extensions that will produce models (term models). One must choose fresh constants (not occurring in prior sentences) for each formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 113A — consistency preserved under adding denumerable constants
rubrics_metrics.description: If Γ is consistent in L and L′ is obtained from L by adding a denumerable set of new constant symbols, then Γ is consistent in L′.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This justification allows expanding the language without introducing inconsistency; it is invoked before adding Henkin constants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 113B — saturated set
rubrics_metrics.description: A set Γ of wffs of a language L is saturated iff for each wff α(x) ∈ Frm(L) with one free variable x there is a constant symbol c ∈ L such that ¬∀x α(x) → ¬α(c) ∈ Γ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saturation formalizes 'every non-universal sentence has a named counterexample' and is the target property for the Henkin expansion process; saturated + complete + consistent sets make the term-model construction work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 113C — construction of the Henkin sentences δn
rubrics_metrics.description: Enumerate all wffs α0(x0), α1(x1), ... with one free variable. For each n pick a fresh constant cn (not occurring in earlier αi or δi) and set δn to be ¬∀xn αn(xn) → ¬αn(cn).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explicit inductive method produces the sequence of Henkin witness sentences to be adjoined iteratively; freshness of constants is essential to the consistency argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 113D — extension to a saturated consistent set
rubrics_metrics.description: Every consistent set Γ can be extended to a saturated consistent set Γ′ by adding the δn Henkin sentences in stages (Γn+1 = Γn ∪ {δn}) and taking the union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof proceeds by induction showing each finite stage is consistent (if Γn ∪ {δn} were inconsistent then Γn would be inconsistent). Uses that the chosen cn do not occur earlier and Theorem 1010A (about replacing fresh constants).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 113E — universals and all closed instances (for saturated sets)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Γ is complete, consistent, and saturated, then ∀x α(x) ∈ Γ iff α(t) ∈ Γ for all closed terms t.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forward direction relies on saturation: if ∀x α(x) ∉ Γ then ¬∀x α(x) ∈ Γ and saturation gives ¬∀x α(x) → ¬α(c) ∈ Γ leading to contradiction. Reverse direction follows from provability of instances and Proposition 112B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 114A (Lindenbaum’s Lemma) — extension to complete consistent set
rubrics_metrics.description: Every consistent set Γ in a language L can be extended to a complete and consistent set Γ∗ by enumerating all sentences α0, α1, ... and at each stage adding either αn (if consistent) or ¬αn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction ensures completeness (for each sentence either it or its negation is eventually added) while maintaining consistency by checking both alternatives and using finite-subset consistency arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 115A — term model A(Γ∗)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given Γ∗ complete, consistent, and saturated (and not yet considering =), define A(Γ∗) with domain the set of all closed terms of L, constants interpreted as themselves, function symbols interpreted by term-formation fA(t1,...,tn)=f(t1,...,tn), and n-place predicate R's extension given by: ⟨t1,...,tn⟩ ∈ RA iff Rt1...tn ∈ Γ∗.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This model is 'covered' (every element is denoted by a closed term) and is designed so atomic sentences are true just in case they belong to Γ∗; it is the main semantic object witnessing satisfiability of Γ∗ (when identity is absent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 115B — evaluation of terms in the term model
rubrics_metrics.description: For the term model A(Γ∗), every closed term t evaluates to itself: t^{A(Γ∗)} = t.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by induction on term-formation; establishes that closed terms name themselves in the term model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 115C — universals in term models via closed instances
rubrics_metrics.description: |=_{A(Γ∗)} ∀x α(x) iff for all closed terms t, |=_{A(Γ∗)} α(t).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the term model is covered (domain = closed terms), checking all closed instances suffices for universal satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 115D (Truth Lemma) — sentences true in term model correspond to membership in Γ∗
rubrics_metrics.description: If α does not contain = then |=_{A(Γ∗)} α iff α ∈ Γ∗.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by structural induction on α (atomic, negation, implication, universal), using earlier propositions (112B, 113E) to relate semantic satisfaction to Γ∗ membership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 116A — equivalence ≈ induced by identity sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: For Γ∗ consistent and complete with identity, define t ≈ t′ iff t = t′ ∈ Γ∗ on the set of closed terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This relation captures which terms are declared equal in Γ∗; used to factor the term model so equal terms denote the same element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 116B — ≈ is an equivalence relation and a congruence
rubrics_metrics.description: Properties: (1) reflexive, (2) symmetric, (3) transitive, (4) congruence for function symbols (replacing a coordinate by an ≈-equal term preserves ≈), (5) predicate compatibility: replacing ≈-equal arguments preserves membership of atomic predicates in Γ∗.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These properties are proved by showing that t = t′ ∈ Γ∗ iff Γ∗ ⊢ t = t′ and using rules for =; they guarantee the quotient construction is well-defined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 116D / Proposition 116E — quotient model A/≈ and well-definedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Define A/≈ with domain Trm(L)/≈ (equivalence classes [t]≈), c^{A/≈} = [c]≈, f^{A/≈}([t1],...,[tn]) = [f t1...tn]≈, and RA/≈ contains ([t1],...,[tn]) iff Rt1...tn ∈ Γ∗; show these definitions do not depend on representative choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 116E (well-definedness) follows from Proposition 116B and induction on arity; ensures A/≈ is a legitimate structure where identity is respected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 116F and 116G — term evaluation and truth lemma for A/≈
rubrics_metrics.description: Lemma 116F: t^{A/≈} = [t]≈. Lemma 116G: For all sentences α (including identity), |=_{A/≈} α iff α ∈ Γ∗.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These complete the argument showing that when identity is present, factoring the term model by ≈ yields a model satisfying exactly the sentences in Γ∗.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 117A — Completeness Theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: If Γ is consistent then it is satisfiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine: extend Γ to saturated consistent set Γ′, then to complete consistent Γ∗ (which will be saturated); construct term model A(Γ∗) (or A/≈ if identity occurs); use the truth lemma to conclude all α ∈ Γ are true in the constructed model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 117B — entailment implies provability (completeness formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: For all Γ and sentences α: if Γ ⊨ α then Γ ⊢ α.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by contraposition: if Γ ⊬ α then Γ ∪ {¬α} is consistent hence satisfiable by completeness, contradicting Γ ⊨ α. Shows equivalence (with soundness) between semantic entailment and syntactic provability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 118A and Theorem 118B — Compactness Theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition: Γ is finitely satisfiable iff every finite Γ0 ⊆ Γ is satisfiable. Theorem (Compactness): (1) Γ ⊨ α iff some finite Γ0 ⊆ Γ entails α. (2) Γ is satisfiable iff it is finitely satisfiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof of (2) given via completeness: finite satisfiability implies every finite subset is consistent, hence Γ is consistent (Proposition 105H), hence satisfiable. Examples illustrate non-expressibility of finiteness, existence of infinitesimals in nonstandard models, and guaranteeing infinitude via sentences α_{≥n}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct proof of Compactness (119-series)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogous Henkin-style construction replacing 'consistent' by 'finitely satisfiable': Proposition 119A (implication behavior for complete finitely satisfiable sets), Lemma 119B (extend finitely satisfiable set to saturated finitely satisfiable set), Proposition 119C (universals ↔ all closed instances for such sets), Lemma 119D (extend to complete and finitely satisfiable Γ∗), and Theorem 119E (Compactness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a proof of compactness without using completeness, by carrying the finite-satisfiability condition through the Henkin/Lindenbaum constructions; crucial steps avoid appeal to ⊢ and instead use model-theoretic finite-satisfaction arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Löwenheim–Skolem Theorems (1110A, 1110B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 1110A: If Γ is consistent then it has a model whose domain is either finite or denumerable (i.e., an enumerable model). Theorem 1110B: If Γ is consistent and contains no identity, then it has a denumerable model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence of the term-model construction: the constructed model's domain is no larger than the set of terms of the language (hence at most denumerable). This yields Skolem's paradox remarks for set theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Many-sorted logic embedding guideline
rubrics_metrics.description: Many-sorted logic (multiple disjoint domains 'sorts') can be embedded in first-order logic by collapsing sorts into one domain, adding unary predicates for sorts, relativizing quantifiers (∀x of sort S becomes ∀x (Sx → ...)), and adding separation/type axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This translation preserves derivations and semantics, giving a completeness theorem for many-sorted logic via first-order completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-order logic: rules, comprehension, and semantics distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Second-order logic extends first-order by variables quantifying over relations; one often adds a comprehension schema ∃R ∀x̄ (α(x̄) ↔ R x̄) for formulas α not containing R. Distinguish (a) minimal/weak second-order derivation systems vs full comprehension, and (b) weak semantics (second-order part big enough to satisfy comprehension axioms) vs full/standard semantics (second-order part = all relations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comprehension is impredicative in full generality; predicative (restricted) comprehension avoids impredicativity. Soundness of comprehension requires ensuring the second-order part of a structure contains the needed relations; full second-order semantics (structures where second-order ranges over all relations) is the usual 'intended' interpretation but is stronger than first-order and changes metatheoretic properties (e.g., completeness fails under full semantics).
